newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal PM rejects EMU "Club Med" label.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal PM rejects EMU "Club Med" label.

text.p: Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres firmly rejected on Tuesday any attempt to lump southern European contenders for a single currency under a "Club Med' label, saying each country must be judged on its merits.

"It would be completely unacceptable if instead of the decision (on monetary union) being taken by political leaders it were taken by a sort of travel agency...based...on the various resorts of the Club Mediterranee," he said.

Guterres, whose government has made qualifying for the European Union's planned economic and monetary union (EMU) its top policy priority, was addressing central bankers gathered in Lisbon to mark the 150th anniversary of the Bank of Portugal.

The Socialist leader mentioned no names, but the reference was clearly to Spain and Italy, often bundled together with Portugal as the so-called "Club Med' countries, a reference to the French holiday operator.

Denouncing any attempt to make links between countries as a violation of sovereignty, Guterres said the only test should be whether a candidate country was economically prepared to join the single currency, due to be launched in 1999.
"What is being tested is the (economic) performance of each country and not that of its neighbours," he said.
Portugal comes a little closer than Spain to meeting the economic conditions laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for entry to EMU and is significantly ahead of Italy.
Its budget deficit will be around four percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year and is forecast to drop to 2.9 percent, inside the three percent EMU ceiling in 1997.

Bank of Portugal governor Antonio de Sousa told central bank chiefs from Germany, France, Brazil and a number of other countries that it was perfectly "achievable" for Portugal to be among the first group of countries in monetary union when it is launched in 1999.
"To achieve it...we need to continue with the macro-economic policies that have enabled Portugal to become a candidate," he said.

In the keynote address to the gathering, European Monetary Institute (EMI) president Alexandre Lamfalussy called for sparing use of the flexibility of interpretation written into the entry tests for monetary union.

Lamfalussy, the head of what will eventually become the European Union's central bank, said that countries should only be regarded as passing tests on state debt and deficits if the figures achieved in 1997 were shown to be sustainable over time.
The Maastricht Treaty says that nations wishing to join monetary union need a budget deficit no higher than three percent of GDP and a debt ceiling of 60 percent.
"We should stick to both the spirit and the letter of the Treaty," Lamfalussy said.
